abar.name: served as a sistrum-player (consecrated musician) in the temple of Amun
abar.notes: Stela V from Kawa records that her father dedicated her as a temple musician of Amun, a role of consecrated royal women.

sources.reference: Kawa Stela V (Taharqa), Macadam, The Temples of Kawa I
Lohwasser, 'Royal Sisters and royal legitimization in the Nubian period'

abar.name: transmits and legitimizes Kushite kingship as King's Mother
abar.notes: As mother of Taharqa and sister-wife of Piye she embodies the maternal line through which 25th-Dynasty royal legitimacy was reckoned; depicted standing behind Taharqa at Gebel Barkal.

sources.reference: Gebel Barkal reliefs of Taharqa; Kawa Stela V
Lohwasser, 'Royal Sisters and royal legitimization in the Nubian period'

akan_aso.name: devises with Anansi the schemes by which he traps his quarry
akan_aso.notes: In the story of winning the sky-god's stories it is Aso, herself wise and cunning, who plans with Anansi the ruse that captures Onini the python.

sources.reference: Rattray, Akan-Ashanti Folk-Tales (1930); Wikipedia, 'Anansi'

abkhaz_antswa.name: sees and knows all things from his dwelling in the sky
abkhaz_antswa.notes: Antswa is conceived as omnipotent, omniscient and wholly good, dwelling in the heavens above the lesser deities he appoints.

sources.reference: Inal-ipa, Abkhazy (Abkhazians); Bgazhba & Lakoba, History of Abkhazia

abkhaz_antswa.name: wields thunder and lightning as his punitive instruments
abkhaz_antswa.notes: Thunder and lightning are reckoned the chastising forces of Antswa, by which he strikes the wicked.

sources.reference: Inal-ipa, Abkhazy (Abkhazians)

abkhaz_afy.name: marks those he strikes with lightning as chosen for the god
abkhaz_afy.notes: A person or beast killed by lightning was held to have been 'visited' and chosen by Afy; such a death was envied as a sign of election.

sources.reference: Inal-ipa, Abkhazy (Abkhazians); Chirikba, on Caucasian lightning cult

abkhaz_aitar.name: presides as a sevenfold deity over the several patrons of individual domestic animals
abkhaz_aitar.notes: Aitar is reckoned a composite or 'sevenfold' divinity grouping lesser patrons such as Jabran (sheep) and Alyshkyntyr (dogs).

sources.reference: Inal-ipa, Abkhazy (Abkhazians); Mythological Encyclopedia (Abkhaz pantheon)

abkhaz_azhwepshaa.name: owns and herds the wild beasts of the forest as master of the game
abkhaz_azhwepshaa.notes: Head of the divine forest-family, owner of herds of deer, elk, fallow-deer and roe, granting their flesh to favoured hunters.

sources.reference: Inal-ipa, Abkhazy (Abkhazians); Religion in Abkhazia (Abkhaz hunting cult)

aboriginal_baiame.name: gives the people their law, marriage rules, songs and rites
aboriginal_baiame.notes: Baiame descended from the sky, ordered the land, and gave the kinship system, mourning customs and hunting taboos.

sources.reference: Howitt, The Native Tribes of South-East Australia (1904)
K. Langloh Parker, The Euahlayi Tribe (1905)

aboriginal_baiame.name: withdraws to and dwells in his sky-camp (Bullimah) after creation
aboriginal_baiame.notes: After shaping Country and instituting law Baiame returned to his sky-home, where he abides as the All-Father.

sources.reference: K. Langloh Parker, The Euahlayi Tribe (1905)

aboriginal_bunjil.name: ascends to the sky-country Tharangalk-bek on a whirlwind of his own raising
aboriginal_bunjil.notes: Having made the land and law, Bunjil had Waang loose the winds, and rose on the whirlwind to dwell in the sky as the headman of the dead.

sources.reference: Howitt, The Native Tribes of South-East Australia (1904)
Smyth, The Aborigines of Victoria (1878)

aboriginal_birrahgnooloo.name: sends the floods and floodwaters when entreated
aboriginal_birrahgnooloo.notes: As All-Mother and senior wife of Baiame she is associated with rain and floodwater and can be petitioned to release floods.

sources.reference: K. Langloh Parker, The Euahlayi Tribe (1905)

aboriginal_birrahgnooloo.name: is mother of the people and of Daramulun in the All-Father complex
aboriginal_birrahgnooloo.notes: Reckoned chief wife of Baiame and mother of all the people; mother of Daramulun in the south-eastern All-Father tradition.

sources.reference: K. Langloh Parker, The Euahlayi Tribe (1905)

aboriginal_binbeal.name: appears as and governs the rainbow
aboriginal_binbeal.notes: Binbeal is the rainbow itself, son of Bunjil; the fainter secondary bow is reckoned his wife.

sources.reference: Smyth, The Aborigines of Victoria (1878)
Howitt, The Native Tribes of South-East Australia (1904)

aboriginal_daramulun.name: speaks through the whirring bullroarer and the thunder
aboriginal_daramulun.notes: The roaring of the bullroarer (often itself called dharamulan) and the rolling of thunder are reckoned the voice of Daramulun.

sources.reference: Howitt, The Native Tribes of South-East Australia (1904)

aboriginal_daramulun.name: presides over the Bora initiation and the knocking-out of the novice's tooth
aboriginal_daramulun.notes: He separates the youths from their mothers, teaches the Burbung/Bora rites and removes a tooth as the mark of initiation.

sources.reference: Howitt, The Native Tribes of South-East Australia (1904)
Mathews, 'The Bora or Initiation Ceremonies of the Kamilaroi Tribe' (1895)

aboriginal_wandjina.name: must have their rock-images repainted to renew the rains and the world
aboriginal_wandjina.notes: The custodians repaint the Wandjina figures to keep their power active and ensure the return of the monsoon and the fertility of Country.

sources.reference: Crawford, The Art of the Wandjina (1968)
Akerman, on Kimberley Wandjina tradition

aboriginal_wagyl.name: is the Noongar Rainbow Serpent, creator and keeper of the fresh waters
aboriginal_wagyl.notes: The Wagyl created the rivers and waterholes of the south-west and was appointed guardian of the rivers, lakes, springs and their wildlife.

sources.reference: Bates, The Native Tribes of Western Australia
State Library of Western Australia, 'The Waugal'

ajaka.name: fosters animal husbandry and the peaceful arts of the herd
ajaka.notes: Unlike his warlike father and brother, Ajaka loved cattle-keeping and encouraged animal husbandry among the Oyo.

sources.reference: Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas

akan_anansi.name: outwits stronger creatures through cunning rather than force
akan_anansi.notes: The Anansesem turn on Anansi defeating the powerful (the python Onini, leopard Osebo, hornets Mmoboro) by wit and trickery.

sources.reference: Rattray, Akan-Ashanti Folk-Tales (1930)

akan_anansi.name: holds ownership of all tales, won from Nyame
akan_anansi.notes: Having paid Nyame's price by capturing the great creatures, Anansi became owner of all stories, so that folktales are called anansesem ('spider words').

sources.reference: Rattray, Akan-Ashanti Folk-Tales (1930)
Britannica, 'Ananse'

akan_komfo_anokye.name: heals and controls nature as the great okomfo (priest)
akan_komfo_anokye.notes: The title okomfo marks his repute as a priest possessed of powers of healing and of command over the natural world.

sources.reference: Britannica, 'Okomfo Anokye'

amani.name: embodies fertility and generative power in his ram-headed Napatan form
amani.notes: The Kushite ram-headed Amun emphasised fertility and martial vigour, conceived as the god in his primeval, generative state.

sources.reference: Kendall, 'Jebel Barkal and Ancient Napata'
Welsby, The Kingdom of Kush

abkhaz_afy.name: fiery arrows of lightning hurled from heaven

sources.reference: Inal-ipa, Abkhazy (Abkhazians)

abkhaz_azhwepshaa.name: his herds of wild deer and forest game

sources.reference: Inal-ipa, Abkhazy (Abkhazians); Religion in Abkhazia

aboriginal_birrahgnooloo.name: the floods and floodwaters at her command

sources.reference: K. Langloh Parker, The Euahlayi Tribe (1905)

aganju.name: ferryman's staff with which he bears travellers across the deep waters

sources.reference: Original Botanica, 'Aganju (Agayu), Orisha of Volcanoes and Wilderness'

akan_tano.name: akrafena state swords kept among his shrine regalia

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Tano (Ta Kora)' (shrine regalia: crown, staffs, swords, beads, brass pan)

akan_tano.name: chiefly crown and beaded regalia of the Tano shrine

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Tano (Ta Kora)'

akan_opoku_ware_i.name: Mponponsuo, the oath-sword of allegiance made for him by Komfo Anokye

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Akrafena' (Mponponsuo made by Akomfo Anokye for Opoku Ware; sword of the oath of office)

akan_osei_tutu_i.name: Bosommuru, the holy state sword on which the Asantehene swears the Great Oath

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Akrafena' (bosommuru: holy sword of the Great Oath, not used for war)

akan_yaa_asantewaa.name: the gun she seized and fired before the chiefs to shame them into war

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Yaa Asantewaa'; Boahen, Yaa Asantewaa and the Asante-British War of 1900-1

amani.gloss: Amun who dwells in the Pure Mountain

sources.reference: Kendall, 'Jebel Barkal and Ancient Napata'

abkhaz_afy.name: the lightning-victim rite (Atlar-chapa)
abkhaz_afy.notes: A person or beast killed by lightning was wrapped in a bull's hide and raised on a platform or tree; kin and villagers dressed in white performed ritual round-dances and choral chants around the body, the death being held an honour.

sources.reference: Inal-ipa, Abkhazy (Abkhazians); Chirikba, on the Caucasian lightning cult

abkhaz_azhwepshaa.name: pre-hunt sacrifice to the lord of game
abkhaz_azhwepshaa.notes: In the hunter's house the elder of the rite held a hazel skewer bearing goat's liver and a glass of wine, with hymns and dances entreating Azhwepshaa to grant the game; the bones of the kill were kept whole so the beast might be revived.

sources.reference: Inal-ipa, Abkhazy (Abkhazians); Religion in Abkhazia (Abkhaz hunting cult)

abkhaz_dzhadzha.name: first-fruits offering of the harvest
abkhaz_dzhadzha.notes: As agrarian goddess of the sown fields she received offerings of the first fruits and of the new grain.

sources.reference: Inal-ipa, Abkhazy (Abkhazians); Mythological Encyclopedia (Abkhaz pantheon)

aboriginal_baiame.name: the Bora initiation ceremony
aboriginal_baiame.notes: Male initiation grounds and ritual sequences re-enacting the ancestral ordering of the world were prepared in Baiame's name across south-eastern Australia.

sources.reference: Howitt, The Native Tribes of South-East Australia (1904)

aboriginal_daramulun.name: the Bora / Burbung initiation
aboriginal_daramulun.notes: At the Bora the bullroarer was sounded as Daramulun's voice, the novices separated from the women and a tooth knocked out; women and the uninitiated were forbidden to see the instrument.

sources.reference: Howitt, The Native Tribes of South-East Australia (1904)
Mathews, 'The Bora or Initiation Ceremonies of the Kamilaroi Tribe' (1895)

aboriginal_wandjina.name: repainting of the Wandjina rock-images
aboriginal_wandjina.notes: Custodians retouch the painted Wandjina figures to renew their potency and call the monsoon rains and the increase of plant and animal life.

sources.reference: Crawford, The Art of the Wandjina (1968)

aganju.name: the festival of Aganju
aganju.notes: An annual festival of drumming, dance and offerings honours Aganju's strength and generative power.

sources.reference: Original Botanica, 'Aganju (Agayu), Orisha of Volcanoes and Wilderness'

akan_asase_yaa.name: the Thursday-rest observance
akan_asase_yaa.notes: As Asase Yaa is 'Earth, of Thursday', the ground may not be tilled or broken on Thursday; she is approached not by temples or idols but by libation and by the oath sworn upon the earth.

sources.reference: Rattray, Ashanti (1923)

akan_tano.name: shrine cult of the Tano (atano)
akan_tano.notes: The river-god is venerated at a chain of shrines (Tanoboase, the Tano Rock, Saaman and others); his principal shrine holds a crown, staffs, state umbrellas, swords, beads and a brass pan, and is the senior of the atano shrines.

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Tano (Ta Kora)'

akan_nyame.name: the Nyame dua (god's tree) household altar
akan_nyame.notes: A forked post cut where three branches meet, set in the compound and holding a pot or basin, at which offerings and libations were made to the otherwise temple-less, non-iconic Sky-God.

sources.reference: Rattray, Ashanti (1923)

amani.name: oracle and coronation cult of Amun of Napata
amani.cadence: at royal accession and on inquiry
amani.notes: At Gebel Barkal the king, as First Prophet of Amun, and the priesthood carried the god's bark in procession to obtain oracular verdicts; Kushite kings were chosen and crowned by the oracle of Amun, as on the stelae of Piye and Aspelta.

sources.reference: Kendall, 'Jebel Barkal and Ancient Napata'
Welsby, The Kingdom of Kush

attributes.name: the lightning-bolt and the thunder-clap
attributes.notes: Afy is manifest in the flash of lightning and the crash of thunder rather than in any anthropomorphic image.

sources.reference: Inal-ipa, Abkhazy (Abkhazians)

sacredAnimals.name: the bull (whose hide shrouds the lightning-struck)

sources.reference: Inal-ipa, Abkhazy (Abkhazians)

attributes.name: the form of the wedge-tailed eagle (eaglehawk)
attributes.notes: Bunjil's defining form is the wedge-tailed eagle; he is also identified with the star Altair, flanked by his two wives the Black Swans (Aquila).

sources.reference: Howitt, The Native Tribes of South-East Australia (1904)
Howitt, The Native Tribes of South-East Australia (1904)

attributes.name: the form of the crow/raven
attributes.notes: Waang appears as the black crow, the trickster moiety-ancestor opposite the eaglehawk Bunjil; the fire he stole and flung blackened his feathers.

sources.reference: Howitt, The Native Tribes of South-East Australia (1904)
Howitt, The Native Tribes of South-East Australia (1904)

attributes.name: large halo-ringed head with great dark eyes and no mouth
attributes.notes: The Wandjina are painted with a white face, immense round eyes, a long nose and no mouth, the head encircled by a halo or band with radiating lines read as cloud, wind and lightning, the body stippled with dots read as rain.

sources.reference: Crawford, The Art of the Wandjina (1968)

attributes.name: the great serpent whose winding body is the rivers and the Darling Scarp
attributes.notes: The Wagyl is a vast rainbow-serpent; its meandering passage carved the Swan and Canning rivers, and the Darling Scarp is reckoned its body.

sources.reference: State Library of Western Australia, 'The Waugal'
State Library of Western Australia, 'The Waugal'

attributes.name: robust regal figure clothed in browns and reds
attributes.notes: Aganju is shown as a powerful kingly figure in earth-brown and fiery red, the colours of volcano and desert.

sources.reference: Original Botanica, 'Aganju (Agayu), Orisha of Volcanoes and Wilderness'
Original Botanica, 'Aganju (Agayu), Orisha of Volcanoes and Wilderness'

attributes.name: the spider and its web
attributes.notes: Anansi's normal form is a spider, though he may take human shape; the web is his emblem of cunning and connection.

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Anansi'
Britannica, 'Ananse'

attributes.name: man with a ram's head crowned with sun-disk and twin plumes
attributes.notes: The Napatan Amun is shown ram-headed, wearing the sun-disk and two tall plumes, his distinctive Kushite form at Gebel Barkal.

sources.reference: Kendall, 'Jebel Barkal and Ancient Napata'

sacredAnimals.name: the ram (and the avenue of ram-headed criosphinxes)

sources.reference: Kendall, 'Jebel Barkal and Ancient Napata'
